***Topics:** moon phases • eclipses (conceptual) • angular size • Kepler’s laws • retrograde motion • empirical laws vs physical explanation*

**Estimated time:** ~3–4 hours

## Why this homework exists (read this)

_This is not busy work._ Astronomy is a “reasoning from evidence” science, and the exams will ask you to explain and apply ideas — not just recall definitions.

This assignment is designed to:

- make the big ideas from Lectures 4–5 stick,
- build the habit of using **geometry and models** to predict what you observe,
- and strengthen the habit of showing reasoning (how you’ll earn points on exams).

---

### What to do

Complete the assigned **Practice Problems** from the end of the following lecture readings:

- **Lecture 4: Moon Geometry** — [Practice Problems]({{< meta params.website-url >}}/modules/module-01/readings/lecture-04-moon-geometry-reading.html#practice-problems)

- **Lecture 5: From Ancient Skies to Kepler’s Laws** — [Practice Problems]({{< meta params.website-url >}}/modules/module-01/readings/lecture-05-keplers-laws-reading.html#practice-problems)

Use the lecture pages for the full problem statements (located at the end of each lecture).

**Note:** You do not need the *Eclipse Geometry* demo for this homework. Use the reading and your own labeled sketches.

## How to earn full credit

{{< include ../_includes/homework/how-to-earn-full-credit.qmd >}}

For this homework, diagrams that are often helpful include a labeled Sun–Earth–Moon sketch, a horizon/zenith sketch, and (for Kepler problems) an ellipse with perihelion/aphelion labeled.

## Pro tips (to save time and pain)

- Start with the conceptual questions first, then do the calculations.
- When stuck, ask: **“What is observable here? What is inferred?”**
- Use **units** as your lie detector.
- Do a quick sanity check: is the answer the right order of magnitude?
